vignette:
Mark used to love the quiet hum of his iMac late at night. It was the sound of creation, of colors and shapes bending to his will. For twenty years as a graphic designer, the late hours were his sanctuary, a time when the world outside fell away and he could build new visual realities on the screen. Now, the silence of the house just makes the other sounds louder: the creak of the floorboards, the rush of a passing car, the frantic thumping of his own heart.

The change began fourteen months ago, on a Tuesday. He was driving home from the studio around 11 p.m., mentally arranging the layout for a new client’s website. He saw the flashing blue and red lights in his rearview mirror before he heard the siren. It was a sudden, violent bloom of color that seared itself into his memory. He pulled over immediately, his mind cycling through the possibilities—a broken taillight? Was he speeding?

The officer’s approach was aggressive, his footsteps heavy on the asphalt. A high-powered flashlight beam cut through the darkness, pinning Mark in his seat. The questions came fast, sharp, and accusatory. Mark’s answers, calm and respectful, seemed only to escalate the officer’s agitation. He was ordered out of the car. Before he could fully process the command, his door was pulled open and he was yanked out onto the pavement. The world tilted—the smell of exhaust, the rough texture of the asphalt against his cheek, the blinding white of the second officer’s headlights. A knee pressed into his back, and the cold, metallic bite of the handcuffs was followed by a searing pain in his shoulder as his arms were wrenched behind him.

He was never told why he was stopped. After ten minutes of terrifying helplessness on the ground, they let him go with a gruff, dismissive warning to “fix his taillight.” Driving home, the car felt like a cage. The familiar streets of his neighborhood seemed alien, filled with unseen threats lurking in the shadows. He didn't tell his wife, Sarah, what really happened. He couldn’t find the words to explain the profound humiliation, the feeling of being utterly powerless.

In the weeks that followed, the world began to lose its color. For a man who lived in a world of Pantone swatches and hex codes, this was a unique kind of hell. The vibrant palettes he once manipulated with ease now felt mocking. How could he design a cheerful brand identity when the world itself had been rendered in grayscale? His work, once a source of pride and flow, became a source of profound anxiety. He’d stare at a blank artboard for hours, his focus shattered by the memory of flashing lights or the imagined sound of heavy footsteps.

Sleep offered no escape, replaying the scene in fragmented, terrifying loops. He’d wake up drenched in sweat, the phantom pain in his shoulder sharp and real. He stopped driving after dark entirely, making excuses to Sarah about being tired. He began sitting with his back to the wall in restaurants, his eyes constantly scanning the room, cataloging exits. The sudden ring of a phone or a knock at the door would send a jolt of pure adrenaline through him.

The distance between him and Sarah grew. He felt a profound sense of detachment, as if he were watching his own life through a thick pane of glass. Her touch, once a comfort, now felt startling. He knew his irritability was hurting her, but the anger was a constant, low-grade hum beneath his skin—an anger at the officer, at the world for being so precarious, and most of all, at himself for being so broken by ten minutes on the side of a road. He spends most of his nights now in his home office, not working, but watching the headlights of passing cars paint fleeting, menacing stripes across the wall.
